# Everest, North Dakota

Everest is an unincorporated populated place in Cass County, North Dakota , . It is a historically significant but sparsely populated settlement whose primary notability stems from its origins as a Great Northern Railroad station in the late 19th century . Located approximately two miles south of the city of Casselton, its history is tied to the expansion of railroads across the American Midwest , . The community's name has a unique origin, derived from a misspelling of the name of Charles A. Everitt, editor of *The Lisbon Star*, rather than being named for the famous mountain . While no longer a thriving community, its official designation in federal geographic databases confirms its existence as a distinct place name , . The area is served by the ZIP code 58723 and falls within the broader Fargo, ND-MN Metropolitan Statistical Area .

## Geography and Administration

Everest is situated within the administrative boundaries of Cass County, North Dakota , . Its precise geographic coordinates are 46°51'35"N latitude and 97°13'26"W longitude, which can also be expressed in decimal degrees as 46.8596957° N and -97.22120059999999° W , , . This specific location places it in the central part of the state, within the civil township that shares its name, Everest Township , . As an unincorporated community, Everest does not possess its own municipal government; instead, local governance and administration fall under the jurisdiction of both Cass County and Everest Township . The U.S. Census Bureau recognizes Everest Township as a county subdivision (cousub) for statistical purposes, confirming its legal and administrative structure within Cass County . This relationship is further supported by the official roster of townships maintained by Cass County government, which includes Everest Township among its listed subdivisions .

A common point of confusion regarding its location arises from some sources incorrectly placing Everest in Divide County, North Dakota . However, definitive geographic data from authoritative federal and state sources resolves this discrepancy. The Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official repository of domestic geographic names maintained by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), classifies Everest as a "Populated Place" in Cass County , . This classification is corroborated by multiple independent datasets, including the North Dakota GIS Hub, which serves as the state's infrastructure for geospatial data, and Randymajors.org, an interactive mapping tool that verifies the placement of civil townships within Cass County , . Therefore, Cass County is the undisputed and correct administrative county for Everest. The community lies along the corridor of Interstate 94 (I-94), a major north-south highway in the United States . Specifically, I-94 passes through the western edge of Everest Township at mile marker 529.007, providing direct road access to the nearby city of Casselton, which is located just four miles to the east . The only named exit on I-94 explicitly associated with Everest Township is Exit 529, which serves the community of Lynchburg .

The postal identity of the area is defined by the ZIP Code Tabulation Area (ZCTA) 58723 . ZCTAs are generalized spatial representations of five-digit ZIP Codes created by the U.S. Census Bureau for the purpose of tabulating and displaying demographic data , . It is important to distinguish ZCTAs from actual USPS mail delivery routes, as they are statistical constructs designed to approximate service areas while protecting individual privacy . Cass County as a whole encompasses 39 different ZIP codes, making 58723 one of several postal districts serving the region . Geographically, Cass County itself is the 10th largest county in North Dakota by total area, covering 1,767.811 square miles, of which 1,764.935 square miles are land . Everest's location within this expansive county provides context for its rural character. The entire area operates under Central Standard Time (CST) . ## History

The history of Everest is intrinsically linked to the westward expansion of the railroad system in the late 19th century. The community was established in 1881 as a station on the Great Northern Railroad . Its founding marked a period of rapid settlement and development in the newly organized territories of the Dakotas. The site was specifically chosen in the northeast quarter of section 15-139-52, located within the boundaries of what would become Everest Township . The establishment of the railroad station likely spurred the creation of a small village, which was officially platted in the same year, 1881 . This development reflects a common pattern of growth where transportation corridors dictated the location of new communities.

A significant milestone in the community's early history was the opening of its post office on May 24, 1882 . The appointment of Carl Knuppel as the first Postmaster signifies the formal recognition of Everest as a settlement with regular communication needs. The post office became a vital hub for the community, facilitating correspondence and commerce during its peak years. However, the reliance on the railroad as the primary driver of economic activity also made the community vulnerable to changes in the industry. The Great Northern Railroad made the decision to remove the station from its operations in 1895, and the physical tracks were subsequently lifted from the ground in 1896 . This event effectively severed the community's main link to the regional economy and likely precipitated its decline. Following the removal of the station, the post office struggled to remain operational. It experienced a temporary closure on August 13, 1904, and another on September 17, 1904, before being permanently closed on November 30, 1908 . With the post office shut down, mail was rerouted to the nearby and more prominent city of Casselton, marking the end of Everest's brief period of active community life .

The historical records provide insight into the community's population trends during its active years. The 1890 United States census reported a population of 175 people living in Everest . This figure indicates a modest but viable settlement during the height of its development. However, subsequent decades saw a dramatic decrease in population. By the 1960 census, the reported population had dwindled to just 10 individuals . This sharp decline suggests that most residents had moved away, leaving behind the structures of the former village. The closure of the post office in 1908 appears to have been the critical turning point that initiated this depopulation. Since 1960, no further census data is available in the provided sources to determine if any inhabitants remained or if the area became completely uninhabited. Despite its sparse population, the community retained its official designation in geographic nomenclature systems, indicating its continued existence as a named place on maps and in official records . The narrative of Everest's history is therefore one of boom followed by bust, a story common to many small railroad-dependent towns that failed to adapt after the industrial shift that the decline of the rails represented.

## Modern Context and Services

In the contemporary era, Everest exists primarily as a historical and geographical designation rather than a functioning community. As an unincorporated populated place, it lacks a local municipal government and does not offer a range of public services that are standard in incorporated towns , . For instance, the North Dakota Department of Public Instruction's official school directory does not list any public or charter schools serving the area of Everest . This implies that any children residing near the former community would need to attend schools in adjacent municipalities. The closest significant educational institutions are located in Casselton, which is served by Central Cass Public School District 17, and potentially in other nearby towns like Kindred, Hunter, and Mapleton, which are served by the Rural Cass Special Education Unit . Given its proximity to Casselton, it is highly probable that residents of the Everest area fall under the jurisdiction of these surrounding school districts.

Information regarding essential utilities such as water, electricity, and emergency services for the immediate vicinity of Everest is not explicitly detailed in the provided sources. However, it is possible to infer the likely service providers based on the broader regional infrastructure of Cass County. Water services in parts of the county are provided by entities such as North Prairie Rural Water . Electrical service is supplied by various utilities operating across North Dakota, including Xcel Energy, Basin Electric, and Central Power, all of which would serve the region . Emergency medical services (EMS) and fire protection would typically be managed by county-wide or multi-township response systems, although specific coverage for the exact coordinates of Everest is not specified. These services are often contracted out to private companies or managed by volunteer departments that cover large rural areas.

The community's connection to the outside world remains intact through modern transportation networks. As previously noted, the presence of Interstate 94 running immediately to the east provides a crucial artery for travel and commerce . The interstate facilitates a short drive to Casselton, which offers a wider array of goods, services, and amenities. Other nearby points of interest include Casselton Robert Miller Regional Airport, located just 1.4 kilometers away, and larger facilities such as Sky Haven Municipal Airport (40 km) and Sheyenne National Grassland (45 km), providing recreational and travel options for residents of the surrounding area . The absence of a permanent population does not render the area entirely isolated; rather, it integrates it into the daily life of the larger Casselton metropolitan area. The community's status is preserved in digital and cartographic form, with its coordinates and designation appearing in official databases like the GNIS and on online mapping platforms, ensuring its place in the geographic record even as its physical footprint may have faded , .

## Demographics

The demographic profile of Everest, North Dakota, is characterized by its small size and a documented history of significant population decline. The most concrete demographic data available pertains to the 1960 United States census, which recorded a population of just ten people in the community . This figure represents a stark reduction from the 175 residents recorded in the 1890 census, highlighting a century-long trend of depopulation following the community's initial establishment and subsequent abandonment . The reasons for this decline are closely tied to the withdrawal of the Great Northern Railroad in 1895 and the closure of the post office in 1908, which likely removed the primary economic incentives for people to live there . Beyond this single data point, the provided sources do not contain any recent census statistics, survey data, or other reliable information detailing the current population, age distribution, household composition, or ethnic makeup of the area. Without data from the 2010 or 2020 censuses, it is impossible to determine if any individuals currently reside within the precise boundaries of the historic community.

To understand the potential demographic context of the area, one must look to the characteristics of its parent entity, Cass County. According to the 2020 U.S. Census, Cass County had a total population of 184,525 people spread across a land area of approximately 1,765 square miles . The county is the second most populous in North Dakota and is part of the Fargo, ND-MN Metropolitan Core Based Statistical Area (CBSA Code 22020), indicating its integration into a larger urbanized region . While the demographic data for Cass County as a whole cannot be directly applied to the uninhabited or nearly uninhabited area of Everest, it provides a backdrop against which the community's sparse nature can be measured. The county's demographic profile would include a mix of urban populations centered around Fargo and more rural populations in townships like Everest Township. The median household income and educational attainment levels for Everest Township could theoretically be found using tools like the randymajors.org map, which links to Census Bureau demographic data for each township, but the specific figures are not included in the provided context blocks . Therefore, any analysis of demographics beyond the known population count from 1960 must remain speculative. The primary takeaway is that Everest is a place with a well-documented history of low population, and its current demographic status remains unknown due to the lack of recent official data collection efforts within its specific, non-incorporated boundaries.

## Etymology

The name "Everest" holds a unique and noteworthy distinction, as it is not named after the world-famous mountain in Asia. Instead, the community was named in honor of a man, Charles A. Everitt, due to a common historical error: a misspelling . This detail provides a compelling backstory that adds a layer of human history to the place's identity. The name was chosen to commemorate Charles A. Everitt, who was identified as the editor of *The Lisbon Star*, a newspaper presumably located in Wisconsin . The act of naming a new community after a respected individual was a common practice during the settlement of the American West, intended to create a sense of stability, progress, and connection to the broader culture of the nation. By honoring Mr. Everitt, the founders of the community likely sought to imbue their new settlement with a similar sense of importance and forward-looking ambition.

The misspelling that led to the name "Everest" instead of "Everitt" is a classic example of how place names can evolve through usage and documentation. Such errors are not uncommon in the chaotic process of frontier settlement, where names were often transcribed from spoken word or handwritten notes, leading to variations that eventually became standardized. The fact that the spelling "Everest" has persisted in official records, such as the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), means that the original misspelling has become the definitive name for the community , . This etymological quirk makes the name itself a piece of history, a tangible remnant of the community's founding era. It separates the North Dakota community from the globally recognized Mount Everest, avoiding any potential confusion and giving it a unique identity rooted in local history rather than international geography. The story of its name underscores the importance of personal connections and the role of media figures like newspaper editors in shaping the cultural landscape of the 19th-century American frontier. The legacy of Charles A. Everitt lives on, not in the pages of *The Lisbon Star*, but in the very name of a small, quiet community in the heart of North Dakota.

Learn About the Domestic Names Committee of the BGN
---------------------------------------------------

#### Background

The Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) is the Federal and national standard for geographic nomenclature. The U.S. Geological Survey's [National Geospatial Program](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/national-geospatial-program) developed the GNIS in support of the U.S. Board on Geographic Names as the official repository of domestic geographic names data, the official vehicle for geographic names use by all departments of the Federal Government, and the source for applying geographic names to Federal electronic and printed products.

The GNIS contains information about physical geographic features of many types in the United States, associated areas, and Antarctica, current and historical, but not including roads and highways or cultural features. The database holds the Federally recognized name of each feature and defines the feature location by state, county, USGS topographic map, and geographic coordinates. Other attributes include names or spellings other than the official name, feature designations, feature classification, historical and descriptive information.

The GNIS Feature ID, Official Feature Name, and Official Feature Location are American National Standards Institute standards as specified in ANSI INCITS 446-2008 (Identifying Attributes for Named Physical and Cultural Geographic Features (Except Roads and Highways) of the United States, Its Territories, Outlying Areas, and Freely Associated Areas, and the Waters of the Same to the Limit of the Twelve-Mile Statutory Zone). The standard is available at the [ANSI Web Store](https://webstore.ansi.org/FindStandards.aspx?SearchString=INCITS+446&SearchOption=0&PageNum=0).

[World](http://wikimapia.org/country/) / [USA](http://wikimapia.org/country/USA/) / [North Dakota](http://wikimapia.org/country/USA/North_Dakota/) / [Casselton](http://wikimapia.org/country/USA/North_Dakota/Casselton/) World / United States / North Dakota

**unincorporated area / community**, **draw only border**

Upload a photo ![Image 1](https://wikimapia.org/img/wm-team-userpic.png)

* * *

Everest is an unincorporated community in Cass County, North Dakota. This was a Great Northern Railroad station built in 1881 in the northeast quarter of section 15-139-52, Everest Township two miles south of Casselton. A village was platted in 1881 and the post office was established May 24, 1882 with Carl Knuppel as Postmaster. A population of 175 was reported in 1890, but the Great Northern Railroad revised their long-range plans, removed this station in 1895, and took up the tracks in 1896. The post office closed August 13, 1904, reopened September 17, 1904, and closed for good November 30, 1908 with mail in both closings going to Casselton. The village existed for many years, reporting a population of 10 as late as 1960. All sources say the town was named for the editor of The Lisbon Star, but his name was actually Charles A. Everitt, not Everest.

[Go to Domestic Names page](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/domestic-names)

Download Names Data
-------------------

The geographic names data provided here contain names for natural features, unincorporated populated places, canals, reservoirs, and more for the United States, its [dependent areas](https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/field/dependent-areas/), and Antarctica. All names data products are extracted from the [Geographic Names Information System (GNIS)](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/what-geographic-names-information-system-gnis), the Federal Government's repository of official geographic names.

#### Accessing Data Using the [The National Map Staged Products Directory](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html?prefix=StagedProducts/GeographicNames/)

All downloadable files are available at [The National Map Staged Products Directory](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html?prefix=StagedProducts/GeographicNames/). The following table contains a description of the downloads available in each geographic names folder. Click the directory title to view the files. An in-depth look at the structure and attribution for each product type is provided in the [GNIS data products document](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/GeographicNames/GNIS_file_format.pdf).

In addition to pipe-delimited text (TXT) files, names data is available in native Geographic Information System (GIS) formats (file geodatabase \[GDB\] and GeoPackage \[GPKG\]) for easier ingest into GIS software and applications. See ['FullModel' below](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/download-gnis-data#FullModel). Each download is a .zip file that contains the data in one of the above-mentioned formats as well as download-specific metadata in an .xml file.

| Directory  | File  
Formats  | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [**Antarctica**](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html?prefix=StagedProducts/GeographicNames/Antarctica/)  | TXT   
GDB  
GPKG | Names data for the continent of Antarctica approved by the [Advisory Committee](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/antarctic-names)  
[on Antarctic Names](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/antarctic-names) of the U.S. Board on Geographic Names. |
| [**Archive**](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html?prefix=StagedProducts/GeographicNames/Archive/)  | TXT  | Static legacy domestic and Antarctica names data last updated August 2021.  
This data will not be refreshed. Includes unmaintained administrative features  
no longer included in GNIS.  |
| [**DomesticNames**](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html?prefix=StagedProducts/GeographicNames/DomesticNames/)  | TXT  | Names data for the 50 States, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S.  
Virgin Islands, Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands. These files are most similar  
to the legacy files previously available for domestic names. Available geographic  
extents are National, States, and AllStates (bundled States). |
| [**FederalCodes**](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html?prefix=StagedProducts/GeographicNames/FederalCodes/)  | TXT  | Domestic names records that have assigned Census codes, Census class  
codes, General Services Administration (GSA) codes, or Office of Personnel  
Management (OPM) codes. Available geographic extents are National,  
States, and AllStates (bundled States). |
| [**FullModel**](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html?prefix=StagedProducts/GeographicNames/FullModel/)  | GDB  
GPKG | _GIS-enabled_ names data for the 50 States, the District of Columbia, Puerto  
Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands. Available  
geographic extents are National and States. |
| [**Topical**](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html?prefix=StagedProducts/GeographicNames/Topical/)  | TXT  | Topical domestic names extracts of GNIS, such as populated places, features  
with description/history, historical features, and government units. Geographic  
extent is National. More information on these data products is [below](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/download-gnis-data#Topical).  |

**Note about character display issues in text files:** GNIS data is maintained in the character set AL32/UTF8 to accommodate native special characters. Names in any language in the Roman alphabet are supported. Some software might not display these characters correctly. Please see the [Unicode Display Problems](https://www.unicode.org/help/display_problems.html) at the [Unicode Consortium website](https://home.unicode.org/) for additional information concerning Unicode character display problems.

[The National Map Downloader. Click to download geographic names and more.](https://apps.nationalmap.gov/downloader/)

#### Other Ways to Explore GNIS Data

Data products are refreshed every other month. To see the latest domestic geographic names, please visit the [GNIS Domestic Names Search Application](https://edits.nationalmap.gov/apps/gaz-domestic/public/search/names). From the application, data on up to 2000 geographic features may be downloaded to a .csv file.

Geographic names downloads described in the table above are also available through [The National Map Downloader](https://apps.nationalmap.gov/downloader/), which provides a user-friendly map interface to help with the selection of your geographic area of interest and desired file format.

GNIS data is also provided as a [National Map web service](https://apps.nationalmap.gov/services/).

[Click here for GNIS metadata.](https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/4f70b292e4b058caae3f8e1d)

Topical Gazetteers
------------------

Topical extracts of GNIS are also available. These files are National in extent and provided in pipe-delimited .txt format. Please click the Gazetteer Type title to begin the download. [Click here](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/GeographicNames/GNIS_file_format.pdf) for an an in-depth look at the structure and attribution associated with each product listed below.

| **Gazetteer Type** | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [**Feature Description /History**](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/GeographicNames/Topical/FeatureDescriptionHistory_National_Text.zip) | Contains only records from the database that have the Description or History fields populated. This layer is meant to be related to the All Names, Populated Places, or Historical Features layers. |
| [**Government Units**](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/GeographicNames/Topical/GovernmentUnits_National_Text.zip) | Contains the names & alphabetic and numerical codes of country, State, and county/county-equivalent governmental units in the database. |
| [**Historical Features**](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/GeographicNames/Topical/HistoricalFeatures_National_Text.zip) | Contains features identified as Historical. A designation of Historical indicates that the name is no longer in use, or the feature no longer serves the original purpose |
| [**Populated Places**](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/GeographicNames/Topical/PopulatedPlaces_National_Text.zip) | Contains features classified as Populated Place in the database. |
| [**All Names**](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/GeographicNames/Topical/AllNames_National_Text.zip) | Contains official and variant names as well as source information for all features. Variant names are non-official names by which a feature is or was known. |

TIGER/Line Shapefile, Current, State, North Dakota, County Subdivision ---------------------------------------------------------------------- Metadata Updated: [August 8, 2025](https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/tiger-line-shapefile-current-state-north-dakota-county-subdivision#sec-dates) This resource is a member of a series. The TIGER/Line shapefiles and related database files (.dbf) are an extract of selected geographic and cartographic information from the U.S. Census Bureau's Master Address File / Topologically Integrated Geographic Encoding and Referencing (MAF/TIGER) System (MTS). The MTS represents a seamless national file with no overlaps or gaps between parts, however, each TIGER/Line shapefile is designed to stand alone as an independent data set, or they can be combined to cover the entire nation. County subdivisions are the primary divisions of counties and equivalent entities for the reporting of Census Bureau data. They include legally-recognized minor civil divisions (MCDs) and statistical census county divisions (CCDs), and unorganized territories. In MCD states where no MCD exists or is not defined, the Census Bureau creates statistical unorganized territories to complete coverage. The entire area of the United States, Puerto Rico, and the Island Areas are covered by county subdivisions. The boundaries of most legal MCDs are as of January 1, 2024, as reported through the Census Bureau's Boundary and Annexation Survey (BAS). The boundaries of all CCDs are those as reported as part of the Census Bureau's Participant Statistical Areas Program (PSAP) for the 2020 Census. ### Access & Use Information **License:** No license information was provided. ### What is the Domestic Names Committee?

The Domestic Names Committee (DNC) of the U.S. Board on Geographic Names (BGN) is responsible for standardizing the names of places, features, and areas within the United States and its [dependent areas](https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/field/dependent-areas/). The DNC consists of members and deputies representing the Departments of the Interior, Commerce, Agriculture, Defense, and Homeland Security, as well as the United States Postal Service, Government Publishing Office, and Library of Congress. The Executive Secretary and staff support for BGN’s domestic names activities and the maintenance of names of Antarctic features are provided by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). The DNC meets [monthly](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/dnc-minutes) to decide on geographic names issues. For more details see the DNC’s [Principles, Policies, and Procedures](https://d9-wret.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/palladium/production/s3fs-public/media/files/DNC_PPP.pdf).

### Domestic Names in the Geographic Names Information System 

[Media ![Image 6: The seal of the Board on Geographic Names, established 1890, featuring a blue and red eagle in front of an Earth illustration](https://d9-wret.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/palladium/production/s3fs-public/styles/side_image/public/thumbnails/image/BGN%20logo_color.png?itok=r2hKzLQv)](https://www.usgs.gov/media/images/seal-us-board-geographic-names)

Sources/Usage: Public Domain. [View Media Details](https://www.usgs.gov/media/images/seal-us-board-geographic-names)

The Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) is the Federal and national standard for geographic names. The U.S. Geological Survey's [National Geospatial Program](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/national-geospatial-program) developed the GNIS in support of the U.S. Board on Geographic Names and to serve as the official repository of domestic geographic names data. GNIS serves as the official geographic names source for all Federal departments and Federal digital and printed products.

##### Find Domestic Names in the GNIS 

Using the [GNIS Domestic Names Search Application](https://edits.nationalmap.gov/apps/gaz-domestic/public/search/names), users can search for names in the database, view the location(s) on various base maps, and link to a more detailed summary page.  The search results can be downloaded.  Help documentation is available with the application.

##### Download Domestic Names 

Domestic Names in GNIS are available for direct download from [The National Map Staged Products Directory](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html?prefix=StagedProducts/GeographicNames/). For more information, go to the [Download GNIS Data](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/download-gnis-data) page. These files are updated every other month.

##### What is in GNIS?

The GNIS contains current and historical information about physical geographic features in the United States, its [dependent areas](https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/field/dependent-areas/), and [Antarctica](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/antarctic-names). The database contains the federally recognized name of each feature and defines its location by State, county, [USGS topographic map](https://www.usgs.gov/programs/national-geospatial-program/topographic-maps), and geographic coordinates. GNIS also lists variant names, which are non-official names by which a feature is or was known. Other attributes include unique Feature ID and feature class. Feature classes under the purview of the U.S. Board on Geographic Names include natural features, unincorporated populated places, canals, channels, reservoirs, and more. Also within GNIS are civil, census, and military features that are maintained via an agreement between the Census Bureau and USGS. [Click here for a full list of domestic names feature classes](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/gnis-domestic-names-feature-classes). Go to [What is the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS)?](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/what-geographic-names-information-system-gnis) for more information.

##### What is _not_ in GNIS?

GNIS does not include roads, highways, administrative, or cultural features. In 2021 the following geographic features referred to as “administrative” (cultural or man-made) were removed from GNIS: airport, bridge, building, cemetery, church, dam, forest, harbor, hospital, mine, oilfield, park, post office, reserve, school, tower, trail, tunnel, and well. Some administrative feature data are maintained in other The National Map data themes. See [The National Map Supporting Themes](https://www.usgs.gov/programs/national-geospatial-program/supporting-themes) page for information on transportation, structures, boundaries, and more.

### Contacts 

If you have questions about the DNC, please contact [BGNExec@usgs.gov](mailto:BGNExec@usgs.gov).

If you have questions about GNIS, please contact [TNM\_Help@usgs.gov](mailto:tnm_help@usgs.gov).

For information on how to submit a proposal to the U.S. Board on Geographic Names for a new name or name change, please see [How Do I?](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/how-do-i)

12.content:
**Title**: Geographic Names Information System Non-Populated Places

**Originator**:  U.S. Department of Interior, U.S. Geological Survey

**Abstract**:

Non-Populated Places is an extract that lists information about large physical and cultural features throughout the U.S. that are described in the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) database. The GNIS database, developed by the U.S. Geological Survey in cooperation with the U.S. Board on Geographic Names, contains information about physical and cultural geographic features in the United States and associated areas, both current and historical, but not including roads and highways. The database also contains geographic names in Antarctica. The database holds the Federally recognized name of each feature and defines the location of the feature by state, county, USGS topographic map, and geographic coordinates. Other feature attributes include names or spellings other than the official name, feature designations, feature class, historical and descriptive information, and for some categories of features the geometric boundaries. The database assigns a unique feature identifier, a random number, that is a key for accessing, integrating, or reconciling GNIS data with other data sets. The GNIS is our Nation's official repository of domestic geographic feature names information. The GNIS is the official vehicle for geographic names use by the Federal Government and the source for applying geographic names to Federal maps and other products. The GNIS supports the U.S. Board on Geographic Names. The Board serves the Federal Government, other government agencies, and the public as the central authority to which name inquiries, name issues, and new name proposals can be directed. The GNIS provides the data to government agencies and to the public. The GNIS also supports the U.S. Geological Survey National Map as the source for the gazetteer search in The National Map viewer and as an active layer in The National Map for Federal boundaries and geographic features not available from state or local sources. Please visit: [https://geonames.usgs.gov](https://geonames.usgs.gov/) for further information.

**Format**: vector points – Shapefile

**Spatial Reference Information**: Decimal Degrees, North American Datum 1983

[Sample map](https://gdg.sc.egov.usda.gov/Catalog/ProductDescription/images/GNISNonP.jpg)

What is the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS)?
=======================================================

The [Geographic Names Information System](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/what-geographic-names-information-system-gnis) (GNIS) was developed by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) in cooperation with the U.S. Board on Geographic Names (BGN), which maintains cooperative working relationships with State Names Authorities to standardize geographic names for Federal use. GNIS contains information about the official names for places, features, and areas in the 50 states, the District of Columbia, and the territories and outlying areas of the United States, including Antarctica. GNIS is the geographic names component of [The National Map](https://www.usgs.gov/programs/national-geospatial-program/national-map).

GNIS contains records for approximately one million geographic names in the United States, including populated places, lakes, streams, summits, valleys, and ridges.

Search GNIS using the [Search Domestic Names](https://edits.nationalmap.gov/apps/gaz-domestic/public/search/names) query form. A feature search yields the official name, State and County, latitude and longitude, the name of the USGS topographic map(s) on which the feature can be found, BGN Decision Date (if relevant), known variant names, and in many cases, additional feature information, i.e., History and Description. There is also an interactive map with optional imagery and other layers.

Learn More: [Geographic Names FAQs](https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names/geographic-names-faqs)

Guide to **Divide County, North Dakota ancestry, genealogy and family history**, birth records, marriage records, death records, census records, and military records. County Information\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: County Information") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: County Information")\] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ### Description\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Description") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Description")\] The county is located in the northwest area of the state.[\[2\]](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy#cite_note-2) ### County Courthouse\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: County Courthouse") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: County Courthouse")\] **Divide County Courthouse** 300 N Main Street PO Box 68 Crosby, ND 58730-0068 Phone: 701.965.6831 [Divide County Website](https://www.dividecountynd.org/?SEC=0193C13B-6272-43A5-8CE1-6FEFF8D53C05) Clerk District Court has birth, marriage, death, burial, divorce, probate and military records from 1910; Register of Deeds has land records from 1910; State Historical Society has naturalization records[\[3\]](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy#cite_note-HBG-3) ### Divide County, North Dakota Record Dates\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Divide County, North Dakota Record Dates") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Divide County, North Dakota Record Dates")\] Information for this chart was taken from various sources, often containing conflicting dates. This information should be taken as a guide and should be verified by contacting the county and/or the state government agency.

Before North Dakota was a state in 1889, parts of North Dakota were included in the 1836 Iowa Territory census (also known as Wisconsin Territory), 1840 Iowa Territory census, 1850 Minnesota Territory census, and the 1860-1880 Dakota Territory censuses.[\[9\]](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy#cite_note-9) See links listed below. #### Territory and State Census Records\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Territory and State Census Records") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Territory and State Census Records")\] * **1836** [1836 Wisconsin Territory Census](http://files.usgwarchives.net/wi/territory/census/1836/1836cens.txt) – index only; North Dakota was included in the 1840 Iowa Territory Census - [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census,_1840_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "United States Census, 1840 - FamilySearch Historical Records") * **1850** [United States Census, 1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638) at [FamilySearch Historical Records](https://familysearch.org/search/) — index & images; North Dakota was included in the 1850 Minnesota Territory Census - [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census,_1850_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "United States Census, 1850 - FamilySearch Historical Records") * **1860** [United States Census, 1860](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1473181) at [FamilySearch Historical Records](https://familysearch.org/search/) — index & images; North Dakota was included in the 1860 Dakota Territory Census - [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census,_1860_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "United States Census, 1860 - FamilySearch Historical Records") * **1870** [United States Census, 1870](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1438024) at [FamilySearch Historical Records](https://familysearch.org/search/) — index & images; North Dakota was included in the 1870 Dakota Territory Census - [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census,_1870_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "United States Census, 1870 - FamilySearch Historical Records") * **1880** [United States Census, 1880](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1417683) at [FamilySearch Historical Records](https://familysearch.org/search/) — index & images; North Dakota was included in the 1880 Dakota Territory Census - [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census,_1880_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "United States Census, 1880 - FamilySearch Historical Records") * **1885** [Dakota Territory 1885 Census Index](http://library.ndsu.edu/db/census/) at [NDSU Archives](https://library.ndsu.edu/ndsuarchives/) – index only * **1885, 1915, 1925** [North Dakota, Territorial and State Censuses, 1885, 1915, 1925](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1078) at Ancestry – - index & images ($) * **1915** [North Dakota Census, 1915](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2346284) at [FamilySearch Historical Records](https://familysearch.org/search/) — index & images - [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/North_Dakota,_Census,_1915_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "North Dakota, Census, 1915 - FamilySearch Historical Records") * **1925** [North Dakota Census, 1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2351024) at [FamilySearch Historical Records](https://familysearch.org/search/) — index & images - [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/North_Dakota,_Census,_1925_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "North Dakota, Census, 1925 - FamilySearch Historical Records") #### Federal Census Records\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: Federal Census Records") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: Federal Census Records")\] Federal Censuses were taken for the state of North Dakota starting in 1890, although no records survived. The 1900 Census is the next Federal Census available. For links to Federal census indexes, see [North Dakota Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/North_Dakota_Census "North Dakota Census"). * [Divide County Census Records](http://www.usgwarchives.net/nd/divide/divicens.htm), USGenWeb Archives ### Church Records\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=16 "Edit section: Church Records") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=16 "Edit section: Church Records")\] Church records can be found online, kept onsite at the church, or housed in a church archive or library. FamilySearch Historical Records"); index, coverage may vary ### Emigration and Immigration\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=19 "Edit section: Emigration and Immigration") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=19 "Edit section: Emigration and Immigration")\] * **1800-1953** [North Dakota, Red River Valley Genealogical Society, Pioneer Files, 1880-1953](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3155904) at FamilySearch — index - FamilySearch Historical Records") ### Ethnic, Political, and Religious Groups\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=20 "Edit section: Ethnic, Political, and Religious Groups") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=20 "Edit section: Ethnic, Political, and Religious Groups")\] ### Funeral Homes\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=21 "Edit section: Funeral Homes") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=21 "Edit section: Funeral Homes")\] ### Genealogies\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=22 "Edit section: Genealogies") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=22 "Edit section: Genealogies")\] ### Guardianship\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=23 "Edit section: Guardianship") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=23 "Edit section: Guardianship")\] ### Land and Property Records\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&veaction=edit§ion=24 "Edit section: Land and Property Records") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=Divide_County,_North_Dakota_Genealogy&action=edit§ion=24 "Edit section: Land and Property Records")\] When the United States acquired North Dakota, most of the land became available for homesteading or purchase from the federal government. After land was transferred from the government to private owners, the registrar of deeds in each county recorded the land transactions in the form of deeds and mortgages. Optionally also show township labels, U.S. city limits and county lines on the map. Also, easily [draw and measure distances](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#drawMeasBtn) and [share your map](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#shareSaveMapBtn). #### Quickly answer ‘What township is this address in’ and ‘What township do I live in’ anywhere in Cass County, North Dakota To find township by address, type the address into the Search places box above the map. ### Quick Tips for using this Cass County, North Dakota Civil Townships map tool 1. There are four ways to get started using this Cass County, North Dakota Civil Townships map tool * **Type an address, city, etc. into the [Search places](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#mapiframe) box above the map** and choose the one you want from the auto-complete list * **Click the map to see the township name for where you clicked** (Monthly Contributors also get [Dynamic Maps](https://www.randymajors.org/access-ad-free-fullscreen-tools#dynamicmaps)) * **Search using GPS coordinates** (latitude and longitude) using the [Find lat long](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#findllinput) box in the top right above the map\* * **Click the [◉ Use Current Location](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#curLocBtn) button** in the upper right corner of the map to use your current location. Click the [◉ Use Current Location](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#curLocBtn) button again to automatically update your location every 1, 5 or 10 minutes ([Monthly Contributors](https://www.randymajors.org/access-ad-free-fullscreen-tools#compare) also get an option to update every several seconds, shown as ◉A for Active).\*\*Township boundary lines will draw on the map, and the township name, state name, country name and latitude/longitude for the blue pin’s location will appear above the map 2. Check the [Show labels](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#leftCheckCont) checkbox in the lower left corner of the map to see the civil township labels on the map 3. Use the [SHOW OTHER LAYERS](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#layercontrolRight) panel in the lower left corner of the map to show county lines, US city limits and US ZIP Codes on the map, overlaid on the civil townships map 4. **[Save your map or Share it](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#shareSaveMapBtn)** with others ##### Learn More * [Draw & Measure distances](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#drawMeasBtn) on the map and [create custom map overlays](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#createmapform) * Explore [Selection Tools](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#about-selection-tools) and view [Census data](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#census-title) * Review [additional usage tips, coverage notes, sources and disclaimers](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#coverage-sources) below * [Subscribe](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#subEmailDiv) to email updates below for tool updates and usage tips * Get Access to expanded funtionality with [Ad-Free Fullscreen Map tools](https://www.randymajors.org/access-ad-free-fullscreen-tools#compare) \* You can search using various formats of latitude longitude, including degrees, minutes and seconds; degrees and decimal minutes; or decimal degrees \*\* The [◉ Use Current Location](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#curLocBtn) button will be more accurate on smartphones and other devices containing a GPS; desktop browsers typically show an approximate location Why would you need a map with civil township boundaries? -------------------------------------------------------- Here are several example uses for civil townships on Google Maps (see [disclaimer](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#disclaimer)): * **Local Governance:** Understanding township boundaries helps residents know which local government they fall under, aiding in civic engagement and accessing township services and resources. * **Land and Property Insights:** For potential land buyers, farmers, and real estate agents, township boundaries provide clarity on land ownership, zoning regulations, and potential utility services. * **Tax Implications:** Different townships might have varying tax rates or structures. Seeing these boundaries aids residents and businesses in navigating local tax responsibilities. * **Historical Context:** Many townships have deep-rooted histories and traditions. Recognizing these boundaries can offer insights into local historical events and regional stories. * **Cultural Exploration:** Just as with cities, townships often have their unique local cultures, festivals, and events. Knowing township borders can enrich cultural experiences. * **Infrastructure Planning:** For urban planners and developers, township boundaries play a pivotal role in understanding local infrastructure needs and future development plans. * **Emergency Response:** In emergencies, knowing township jurisdictions ensures a coordinated and swift response from local emergency services. * **Business Opportunities:** Entrepreneurs can strategize better by recognizing township boundaries, considering local needs and preferences. * **Environmental Studies:** Researchers looking into local ecosystems, farming practices, or conservation efforts can benefit from clearly defined township areas. * **Educational Relevance:** Educators and students studying local geography, governance, or history can leverage township maps for a clearer understanding of the subject matter. * **Community Building:** Grassroots movements, community organizers, and local NGOs can focus their efforts more effectively within specific townships. * **Transport and Connectivity:** For logistics and transportation businesses, township boundaries can be crucial for route planning, especially in rural or semi-rural areas. ### Census Bureau Statistics #### Click the [township names](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#mapdiv) above the map to show the following Census demographic data for the civil township the blue pin is located in Census data is available for U.S. cities, counties, civil townships and ZIP Codes. ![Image 2](https://www.randymajors.org/wp-content/uploads/icons/people.svg) Populations and People Total Population ![Image 3](https://www.randymajors.org/wp-content/uploads/icons/income.svg) Income and Poverty Median Household Income ![Image 4](https://www.randymajors.org/wp-content/uploads/icons/education.svg) Education Bachelor’s Degree or Higher ![Image 5](https://www.randymajors.org/wp-content/uploads/icons/employment.svg) Employment Employment Rate ![Image 6](https://www.randymajors.org/wp-content/uploads/icons/housing.svg) Housing Total Housing Units ![Image 7](https://www.randymajors.org/wp-content/uploads/icons/health.svg) Health Without Health Care Coverage ![Image 8](https://www.randymajors.org/wp-content/uploads/icons/family.svg) Families and Living Arrangements Total Households ![Image 9](https://www.randymajors.org/wp-content/uploads/icons/race.svg) Race and Ethnicity Hispanic or Latino (of any race) ### Selection Tools: Find Civil Townships by radius or by drawing a line or shape 1. **Click the [Selection Tools](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#selToolsBtn) button** in the lower left corner of the map 2. – RADIUS SELECT: To find Townships within a radius, specify the mileage in the “Optional radius select” box, then use the Point “Add a marker” tool to drop the center point of the radius.\* While using the Point “Add a marker” tool, you can also use the [Search places](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#mapiframe) box to select Townships within a radius of an address, or use the [Find lat long](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#findllinput) box to select Townships within a radius of a given latitude longitude. – SELECT USING A LINE OR SHAPE: To find Townships that _touch_ a line or a shape you draw, use the Line tool or Shape tool to draw the shape, double-clicking when finished\* – SELECT WITHIN DISTANCE OF A LINE OR SHAPE (also known as a buffer): To find Townships that are _within a distance_ of a line or a shape you draw, first specify the mileage in the “Optional radius select” box, then use the Line tool or Shape tool to draw the shape, double-clicking when finished\* 3. The Townships and township limits will be highlighted and listed in a “Results from map” box below the map, where you can copy the selected Townships for use in a spreadsheet or other document – Optionally, keep drawing shapes to select more Townships 4. When you are finished selecting Townships, click the “Done Selecting” button in the lower left corner of the map \* Townships will get selected if any part of the shape you draw (or applied radius or buffer) falls within the township boundaries ### FAQs for Cass County, North Dakota - Townships Map Does Google Maps show Cass County, North Dakota township boundaries? [This Cass County, North Dakota civil townships map tool](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show) shows Cass County, North Dakota township boundaries on Google Maps. You can also show township name labels on the map by checking the box in the lower left corner of the map. How do I view an interactive map of Cass County, North Dakota township boundaries or town lines? [This Cass County, North Dakota civil townships map tool](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show) shows Cass County, North Dakota township boundaries on Google Maps. Other tools on this website also show city limits, townships, section township range, ZIP Codes, elevation and more. Why might I need to know the Cass County, North Dakota township for a given place or address? You might need to [know the Cass County, North Dakota township for an address](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show) to: - determine applicable laws or regulations based on township jurisdiction - determine what Cass County, North Dakota township an address is located in or if it is outside of a township - determine what county or counties a township is located in - record township information when conducting field research using GPS coordinates (see \* above) - perform volunteer work based on township - perform emergency dispatch based on township - calculate the correct local township sales tax How do I find Cass County, North Dakota township by address? To find the Cass County, North Dakota township for an address, type the address in the [Search places](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#mapiframe) box above [this Cass County, North Dakota civil townships Finder map tool](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show). the Cass County, North Dakota township name appears near the top of the map and the blue dot shows the location of the address on the map. What is my Cass County, North Dakota township? What Cass County, North Dakota township do I live in? To find your Cass County, North Dakota township using your address, type your address in the [Search places](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#mapiframe) box above [this map](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show). ### Additional Usage Tips * Be sure to read the [Quick Tips](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#how-to-use) above on how to use this map tool * In the upper right corner of the map, you can switch the map between [Map view (with optional Terrain), Satellite view or POI view (points of interest)](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#mapiframe) * As you zoom in, highways, roads, streets and other map features are also shown on this Civil Township map * The [Search places](https://www.randymajors.org/civil-townships-on-google-maps?fips=38017&labels=show#mapiframe) box uses a standard Google Maps geocoding engine, therefore you can type street addresses, road names, points of interest, etc. to see what township that location is part of – Note that typing an address will zoom in the map very close, whereas typing a city or township by itself will show you a map with a wider view * Because the map layers are complex, boundaries will not be shown if you are zoomed out too far * [Search the FAQs](https://www.randymajors.org/help#searchHelpInput) for more detailed help #### Coverage Notes * Civil townships includes the boundaries of [Civil townships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_township), also called township limits, town lines, or township borders. New England, New York and Wisconsin typically refer to townships as towns, and Michigan uses charter townships.Townships with the following US Census Bureau minor civil division (county subdivision) class codes are shown: – T1: Governmentally active [minor civil division (MCD)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_civil_division) or county subdivision that is not coextensive with an incorporated place (this is often a township) – T5: An active county subdivision that is coextensive with an incorporated place – T9: An inactive county subdivision – Z1: A nonfunctioning county subdivision – Z2: A county subdivision that is coextensive with an American Indian, Alaska Native, or Native Hawaiian area and legally is independent of any other county subdivision – Z3: A county subdivision defined as an unorganized territory #### Civil Township boundaries depicted include the following types of townships for each state

ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs)
=================================

ZIP Code Tabulation Areas or ZCTAs (pronounced _zik-tahs_) are a geographic product of the U.S. Census Bureau created to allow mapping, display, and geographic analyses of the United States Postal Service (USPS) Zone Improvement Plan (ZIP) Codes dataset.

### ZIP Codes versus ZCTAs

First introduced in 1963, ZIP Code is a trademark of the USPS created to coordinate mail handling and delivery. The USPS assigns ZIP Code ranges to regional post offices, which in turn assign ZIP Codes to delivery routes. Each delivery route is composed of street networks, and/or individual units with high mail volumes, such as high-rise buildings or individual business locations. Within the Census Bureau’s MAF/TIGER System, ZIP Codes are stored as one component of discrete addresses tied to delivery points, including specific housing unit locations. The result is a point-based dataset unsuitable for mapping and many analysis applications.

ZCTAs are generalized areal representations of the geographic extent and distribution of the point-based ZIP Codes built using 2020 Census tabulation blocks. The Census Bureau is restricted by Title 13 from releasing individual housing unit addresses or location information to the public, so point-based ZIP Code data are unsuitable for distribution and publication. However, by aggregating the points and extrapolating them to a polygonal-based unit (census tabulation blocks), disclosure concerns can be addressed and “geographic subtraction[](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/guidance/geo-areas/zctas.html#_ftn1)\*” is prevented.

[](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/guidance/geo-areas/zctas.html#_ftnref1)\* “Geographic subtraction” is the comparison of data for overlapping geographic areas to identify the location and characteristics of individual respondents and housing units. This can inadvertently result in data disclosure and is a major concern for geography representing a relatively small area (below county level) or geography with low counts of population or housing units.

### Summary of 2020 ZCTA Delineation Methodology

*   Each assigned 2020 Census tabulation block is part of one distinct 2020 ZCTA.
*   All 2020 ZCTA Codes are current valid USPS ZIP Codes (as of January 1, 2020).
*   Not all valid ZIP Codes are represented by a 2020 ZCTA.
*   For tabulation blocks that contain housing units, the ZCTA represents the ZIP Code associated with the most addresses in that block.
*   All inhabited areas have 2020 ZCTA coverage.
*   2020 ZCTA coverage includes zero population blocks that are enclosed within a ZCTA, located along the fringes of a ZCTA, or form a small gap between ZCTAs.
*   Uninhabited areas (land and water areas) over two square miles are potentially left unassigned from 2020 ZCTA coverage.
*   2020 ZCTAs may form noncontiguous areas (e.g., islands or enclaves).
*   A 2020 ZCTA may represent a single institutional or corporate delivery point address.
*   2020 ZCTAs may represent mixed mail delivery (non-unique), firm or organization-specific (unique), or post office box-only (PO Box) ZIP Codes.
*   All 2020 ZCTA boundaries are 2020 Census tabulation block boundaries.

### Comparison of 2020 Census ZCTAs to 2010 Census ZCTAs

The delineation methodology used for the 2020 Census ZCTAs are identical to those used for the 2010 Census ZCTA delineation.

| **Interstate 94** (**I-94**) runs east–west for 352.4 miles (567.1 km) through the southern half of the US state of [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota"), from the [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana") state line east to the [Red River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_of_the_North "Red River of the North") at [Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo,_North_Dakota "Fargo, North Dakota"). The route generally follows the route of the [Northern Pacific Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Pacific_Railway "Northern Pacific Railway"). Route description ----------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Interstate_94_in_North_Dakota&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Route description")\] Eastbound, the route enters from [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana") just west of [Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beach,_North_Dakota "Beach, North Dakota") and passes [Dickinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickinson,_North_Dakota "Dickinson, North Dakota"), [Bismarck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bismarck,_North_Dakota "Bismarck, North Dakota"), [Jamestown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamestown,_North_Dakota "Jamestown, North Dakota"), [Valley City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_City,_North_Dakota "Valley City, North Dakota"), and [West Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Fargo,_North_Dakota "West Fargo, North Dakota") before entering [Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo,_North_Dakota "Fargo, North Dakota"), where it exits the state at the [Red River of the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_of_the_North "Red River of the North") and continues into [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota") at [Moorhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorhead,_Minnesota "Moorhead, Minnesota"), then turns southeast to [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis"). The route passes to the south of [Theodore Roosevelt National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt_National_Park "Theodore Roosevelt National Park")'s southern unit; access to the northern unit is by [US Highway 85](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_85_in_North_Dakota "U.S. Route 85 in North Dakota") (US 85) north from [Belfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfield,_North_Dakota "Belfield, North Dakota"). Eastbound, I-94 changes [timezones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_the_United_States "Time in the United States") at the [Stark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stark_County,_North_Dakota "Stark County, North Dakota")–[Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morton_County,_North_Dakota "Morton County, North Dakota") county line southwest of [Hebron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebron,_North_Dakota "Hebron, North Dakota"). [Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_Time_Zone "Mountain Time Zone") time (UTC−7) is observed in Stark County (and west) and [Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone") time (UTC−6) in the rest of the state. The speed limit on I-94 is 80 mph (130 km/h) in rural areas. Between exits 152 and 161 in the Bismarck–Mandan area, the speed limit is 60 mph (97 km/h). In the West Fargo–Fargo area, the speed limit is 65 mph (105 km/h) at mile 345, and 55 mph (89 km/h) from exit 346 to the Red River of the North. I-94 has two lanes in each direction through most of the state, expanding briefly to three lanes in each direction in the Bismarck–Mandan area (from exit 155 to 156) and in Fargo from 45th Street (exit 348) to the Red River of the North. The [elevation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevation "Elevation") of the highway at the [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana") border is approximately 2,820 feet (860 m) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"), and approximately 900 feet (270 m) at its crossing of the north-flowing [Red River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_of_the_North "Red River of the North"), entering Minnesota at Moorhead. ### Points of interest \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Interstate_94_in_North_Dakota&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Points of interest")\] The route enters at [Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beach,_North_Dakota "Beach, North Dakota") and passes through the [badlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badlands "Badlands") near [Medora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medora,_North_Dakota "Medora, North Dakota") and the south unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park. A public rest area about seven miles (11 km) east of Medora provides an awe-inspiring view, especially at sunset, and an opportunity to hike through some of the scenery on the Painted Canyon Trail. Further east, I-94 provides access to the north unit of the national park, then passes through the cities of Dickinson, Mandan–Bismarck, Jamestown, and [Valley City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_City,_North_Dakota "Valley City, North Dakota") on the way to West Fargo and Fargo, where it leaves the state and crosses into Minnesota. Through North Dakota, I-94 travels nearly due east–west, generally following both the [railroad route](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Pacific_Railway "Northern Pacific Railway") and the former route of [US 10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_10_in_North_Dakota "U.S. Route 10 in North Dakota") (called "The Old Red Trail" or "The National Parks Trail") to exit 343 in West Fargo, where the current US 10 has its western terminus. The highway intersects with the [Enchanted Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enchanted_Highway "Enchanted Highway") 11 miles (18 km) east of Dickinson at exit 72. At [New Salem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Salem,_North_Dakota "New Salem, North Dakota"), it passes [Salem Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salem_Sue "Salem Sue"), a 38-foot-high (12 m) sculpture of a [Holstein cow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holstein_cow "Holstein cow") that is clearly visible on the south side of the highway; the road to Sue allows a vantage point to view a panoramic landscape. Between Mandan and Bismarck, I-94 crosses the [Missouri River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River") with a view of the Northern Pacific (now [BNSF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BNSF_Railway "BNSF Railway")) Railway Bridge to the south. At [Steele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steele,_North_Dakota "Steele, North Dakota"), it passes the world's largest sculpture of a [sandhill crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandhill_crane "Sandhill crane"), 40 feet (12 m) tall and named "Sandy", on the south side of I-94, just east of exit 200. At Jamestown, it passes the world's largest sculpture of a [buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World%27s_Largest_Buffalo "World's Largest Buffalo") (actually [bison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bison "Bison")) named "Dakota Thunder", 28 feet (8.5 m) in height and on the north of the highway. Valley City is known for its nickname, "City of Bridges", and is home to the [Hi-Line Railroad Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi-Line_Railroad_Bridge "Hi-Line Railroad Bridge"). [![Image 22](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Continental_Divide_Sign.jpg/250px-Continental_Divide_Sign.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Continental_Divide_Sign.jpg) [Laurentian Divide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurentian_Divide "Laurentian Divide") sign, westbound on I-94 At approximately milemarker 275 on the westbound lanes between Jamestown and Valley City, the highway crosses the [Laurentian Divide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurentian_Divide "Laurentian Divide"), at an [elevation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevation "Elevation") of 1,490 feet (450 m) [above sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_sea_level "Above sea level"). The rivers that are west of this divide flow south into the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") from the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico"), while the rivers that are east of the divide flow north into [Hudson Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay "Hudson Bay"). The [James River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_River_/(Dakotas/) "James River (Dakotas)"), that flows through Jamestown, feeds into the Atlantic Ocean, while the [Sheyenne River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheyenne_River "Sheyenne River"), that flows through Valley City (36 miles (58 km) east of Jamestown), feeds into Hudson Bay. In Fargo, a well-known yet unnamed [pedestrian bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedestrian_separation_structure "Pedestrian separation structure") crosses over I-94; opened 49 years ago in 1976, in time for the [US Bicentennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Bicentennial "US Bicentennial"). While providing a unique crossing for the surrounding neighborhoods, it serves as a landmark for commuters and travelers. Westbound, it is one of the first North Dakota landmarks visible from the highway.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94_in_North_Dakota#cite_note-Kerzman-2) History ------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Interstate_94_in_North_Dakota&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: History")\] [![Image 23](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/NDI94.jpg/250px-NDI94.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NDI94.jpg) East bound on I-94, the main highway east–west through North Dakota[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94_in_North_Dakota#cite_note-3) Through the state, I-94 follows the route once taken by [US 10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_10_in_North_Dakota "U.S. Route 10 in North Dakota") west from [Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo,_North_Dakota "Fargo, North Dakota"). This route was originally called "The Old Red Trail". [Prairie Public Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prairie_Public_Television "Prairie Public Television") in North Dakota produced a documentary about US 10 and the building of I-94 through the state.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] I-94 roughly follows the route of the former [Northern Pacific Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Pacific_Railway "Northern Pacific Railway") mainline (now a [BNSF Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BNSF_Railway "BNSF Railway") route) across North Dakota. Many of the towns and cities that I-94 serves first grew as railroad towns in the 19th and early 20th centuries.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] The first section of I-94 completed with funds from the [Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal-Aid_Highway_Act_of_1956 "Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956") was a 39-mile (63 km) section between Jamestown and Valley City. It was opened on October 16, 1958, and cost $15 million (equivalent to $125 million in 2024[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94_in_North_Dakota#cite_note-inflation-USGDP-4)) to construct.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94_in_North_Dakota#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94_in_North_Dakota#cite_note-6) On October 7, 1964, a 112-mile (180 km) section of I-94 between [North Dakota Highway 25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota_Highway_25 "North Dakota Highway 25") and Fryburg was dedicated, with traffic permitted to use the section from New Salem to Dickinson.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94_in_North_Dakota#cite_note-7) Future ------ \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Interstate_94_in_North_Dakota&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Future")\] In January 2024, the North Dakota Department of Transportation (NDOT) announced that they had begun a study to replace the Grand Marsh Bridge over the [Missouri River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River") in [Bismarck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bismarck,_North_Dakota "Bismarck, North Dakota"). The bridge was built in 1965 and has not seen any major improvements since that time. NDOT engineers will look into what some possible replacements for the bridge could be, including the possibility of demolishing the bridge and replacing it with a tunnel. NDOT also said that the study will also include improving some of the ramps and surrounding roadways. The study is projected to be completed by the end of the year.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94_in_North_Dakota#cite_note-8) Exit list ---------
